title: Jury urges changes at jail: Three recommendations come after inquest into death of prisoner
article: Police procedure in handling suspects taken into custody must be improved and tightened, the jury in the coroner's inquest into the death of Craig James Morency recommended Friday.

After deliberating for two hours at Ontario Superior Court, the five jurors returned with a finding the 34-year-old Windsor man, who died at Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital hours after being arrested and put in jail for breaking into a car, was killed by morphine toxicity. His death, June 22, 2004, was ruled accidental, the result of a broken bag of drugs he had ingested earlier.

\- Better communication. This would include officers giving advance notice to cell block personnel if an increase is expected in jail population due to circumstances such as mass arrests, raids or an unusually high number of remand transfers.
The suggestion followed inquest evidence that Morency overdosed in jail unnoticed when the cell block was busy and crowded because of arrests made during a drug bust.
In such cases where there is an unusually high number of inmates to process, the jury further recommended that extra officers be called in to deal with the situation and maintain normal procedures.

\- The jury called for additions to prison registration forms. They recommended any unusual occurrence during prisoner transport be verbally reported then logged on a personal prisoner check sheet to ensure all important information is passed along to the detention officer.

This stems from evidence that the officer who transported Morency to police headquarters noticed he had gotten his hands out from behind his back during the ride and had possibly freed one wrist from the handcuffs. Testimony suggested that Morency might have struggled free to ingest the morphine during the trip to avoid drug charges.

\- Jurors suggested that new personal security check sheets be implemented to ensure each prisoner is charted on a record of incarceration to allow for personalized observation. The new check sheet would include the question, have you consumed alcohol or drugs recently?

Lawyer Craig Allen, who represented Morency's family -- which includes his estranged common-law wife and their 10-year-old son -- said the recommendations showed the jurors agreed that Morency, while being transported to the jail, may have freed his hands enough to swallow the bag of drugs. Other evidence suggested he might have swallowed the drugs in a coffee shop washroom just prior to arrest.
"I believe the jury followed the evidence closely to reach their conclusions," he said. "Hopefully those in government will consider the recommendations seriously and implement them."
Coroner William Buckton said the verdict and recommendations would be forwarded to "the appropriate government ministries and Ontario's Chief Coroner's office" for study and possible implementation.

Tests showed Morency had 1,178 nanograms of morphine per millilitre of blood at the time of his death. Morency was arrested at a Tim Hortons near Wyandotte Street and Lauzon Road after he was seen breaking into a car. Upon arrest he was frisked and placed in a police transport van with his hands cuffed behind his back.
He was discovered in his cell about seven hours later, covered in orange vomit and unresponsive. He was rushed to hospital where he died.
